role: Early companion and servant of the Prophet ﷺ
Senior scholar of Quran and fiqh in Kufah
summary: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA) was among the earliest Muslims, the sixth person to accept Islam according to several classical accounts. He served as a close personal attendant of the Prophet ﷺ, was the first to recite the Quran publicly in Makkah, and became the foremost Quranic authority of his generation. His school of Quranic interpretation and fiqh in Kufah shaped the entire Hanafi legal tradition through his students.
biography:
Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ibn Ghafil al-Huzali was born in Makkah around 594 CE, from the tribe of Hudhayl, allied with the Quraysh but not themselves Qurayshi. He came from modest means and worked as a shepherd for the Quraysh chieftain Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt before the beginning of prophethood. In the early Makkan period, he encountered the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and immediately accepted Islam, making him among the very first Muslims — classical scholars debate whether he was the sixth, seventh, or among the first ten to accept, but his early seniority is beyond dispute. Ibn Sa'd records in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (Vol. 3) that Ibn Mas'ud was so close to the Prophet ﷺ that he attended to his personal needs — his sandals, his walking stick, his purification — and was effectively part of the Prophet's household.

Ibn Mas'ud made the first Hijrah to Abyssinia with the persecuted early Muslims, returned to Makkah, and subsequently made the Hijrah to Madinah. He was present at the Battle of Badr, Uhud, and all the major campaigns. At Badr, the narration in Sahih al-Bukhari (Kitab al-Maghazi) records that Ibn Mas'ud killed or captured the Quraysh leader Abu Jahl — the Prophet ﷺ confirmed this and honored him for it.

His supreme legacy, however, was in the Quran. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Take the Quran from four persons: Ibn Mas'ud, Salim (the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfah), Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Fada'il al-Quran). This direct prophetic designation made Ibn Mas'ud among the four primary authorities on Quranic recitation in the first generation. He was also the first companion to recite the Quran publicly in Makkah before the Hijrah — an act of extraordinary courage given the Quraysh's hostile response to the Quran. Standing near the Ka'bah, he recited Surah al-Rahman aloud to the assembled Quraysh nobles, who beat him until his companions had to pull him away. Al-Dhahabi records this episode in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' (Vol. 1) as one of the earliest acts of Quranic da'wah.

The depth of Ibn Mas'ud's Quranic knowledge was extraordinary. He narrated: 'By Allah, besides Whom there is no god, there is no surah in the Book of Allah about which I do not know where it was revealed, and there is no verse about which I do not know why it was revealed.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Fada'il al-Quran). He memorized 70 surahs directly from the mouth of the Prophet ﷺ himself, a fact he emphasized throughout his scholarly career.

During the caliphate of Umar (RA), Ibn Mas'ud was sent to Kufah as a teacher and treasurer, with Umar writing to the people of Kufah: 'I have sent you Ammar ibn Yasir as governor and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud as teacher and minister. They are among the elite companions of the Prophet ﷺ who fought at Badr. Learn from them and obey them.' (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat, Vol. 3; al-Dhahabi, Siyar, Vol. 1). Ibn Mas'ud settled in Kufah and his school there became the foundation for what would later be systematized as the Hanafi legal tradition by Imam Abu Hanifa's teachers. The great Kufi scholar Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and others transmitted the fiqh and Quranic methodology of Ibn Mas'ud to successive generations.

His hadith transmission was prolific. Al-Dhahabi counts approximately 848 narrations attributed to him in the major collections. His narrations span Quranic exegesis, jurisprudence, and personal descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ. Among the most cited of his narrations is the famous hadith on the perfection of knowledge: 'Shall I not tell you what knowledge really is? It is humility.' And the hadith on truthfulness: 'Hold fast to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Adab; Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Birr wal-Silah)

Ibn Mas'ud experienced tensions during the caliphate of Uthman (RA), particularly around the standardization of the Quranic Mus-haf, where his own mushaf variant was among those that were collected in favor of the standardized text compiled from the recitation of Zayd ibn Thabit. Classical scholars including al-Dhahabi acknowledge this disagreement but record that Ibn Mas'ud ultimately accepted the consensus of the companions on this matter. He died in Madinah in 32 AH (approximately 653 CE) during the caliphate of Uthman (RA) and was buried in the Baqi' cemetery.
